Then she did the next problem from scratch, splitting the velocity into components first, finding the vertical part, halving her old method in reverse, doubling at the end. It was not a trick, she decided; it was more like a grammar. Once you knew the rules, you could codify them into a procedure and stop worrying about the shape of every individual throw.

She said this out loud, more or less, and Liberty shrugged. "It's a rule until it isn't. We ignored air resistance to get it, so it's a lie we agreed on."

That was the part Mackenzie could not settle. The problems all ended with the same small phrase, neglecting air resistance, and outside the binder nothing neglected anything. Luc's board fought the wind. A fried napkin tumbled sideways off the bench. The clean doubling, the perfect symmetry of rise and fall, belonged to a world that had been simplified on purpose so that it could be solved at all, and she could not decide whether that made it beautiful or make-believe.

Luc pushed up out of the bowl and crossed the concrete toward them, board underfoot until the last second, then in his hand. His shirt was dark with sweat and he was grinning in a way that meant the kickflip had finally landed. "Give me a fry," he said, and then, seeing her binder, "What's that face? You look like the numbers lost."

"The numbers won. It's the world that's arguing." She turned the binder toward him and pointed at the parabola. "If I throw your board straight up at ten meters per second, it takes about one second going up. How long coming down?"

Luc looked at the ramp behind him, then at the sky, chewing. "One second. Same."

"That's what the book says. Rising and falling take equal times, so the whole flight is twice the vertical velocity over g." She closed the binder. "But throw it for real and it comes down slower, drag eats it, and the book just pretends that away."

"So which is true?"

"Both, in different rooms." She stood, picked up the bag of fries, and held it out to him. He took two and put the whole second one in his mouth at once. Down in the bowl another skater dropped in, wheels hammering the transition, and Mackenzie stood there listening to the long rise and fall of it, counting under her breath, "One. Two."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
The parking lot behind Gagnon Driving Academy still held the morning's frost in its shadowed corners, and Alexis sat in the driver's seat with his hands at ten and two, waiting for the instructor to finish writing on her clipboard. His grandfather had driven him here, and had spent the whole ride delivering his advice like scripture: pump the brakes in an emergency, tap and release, tap and release, the way he had learned in 1974. "Write that down," his grandfather had said at the curb, and Alexis had not written it down, but he remembered it anyway, the way you remember things you half doubt.

"Foot on the brake, shift into drive, and ease out of the spot," the instructor said. Her name was on the lanyard but he had already lost it. "Steering's light. Don't fight it."

The car crept forward. Everything about it felt borrowed, the seat still shaped to the last student, the mirrors angled for someone shorter. Alexis steered around the orange cones at walking speed while she talked about blind spots, and he found that he could listen and drive at the same time only if he let her words arrive half heard, the way lyrics arrive on a bus.

At the second row of cones she said, "Faster this time. Fifteen, twenty." The lot ended at a chain-link fence with a faded sign about unauthorized vehicles. When he accelerated, the wheel woke up under his hands, and the whole car seemed to tilt toward consequence. She waited until he was midway down the lane, then said, "Stop. Now."

He stamped the pedal and the car surged, nose diving, tires dragging on the cold asphalt, and he pumped. Tap and release, tap and release, because his grandfather's voice was closer in his head than hers. The car traveled far enough that the fence filled the windshield before it finally shuddered still.

"Where'd you learn that?" she asked. Not angry. Curious, almost.

"My grandfather. Pump the brakes."

"That's the old way. This car has anti-lock brakes. In an emergency you press the brake firmly and hold it, and you can still steer while you're braking." She set the clipboard on her lap. "Try it again. Same speed."

He circled the cones. His face was warm and he kept his eyes on the fence on purpose, refusing to glance at her, because a glance would have been an invitation to discuss it. Coming down the lane she said, "Stop," and this time he pressed hard and held, and the pedal buzzed under his foot like something alive, and the car pulled up short with room to spare, and though the whole event lasted three seconds he had never felt so completely present inside one.

"See? Firm and hold. You can steer through it too, which you couldn't do with the wheels locked." She was already noting something on her clipboard. "Grandfather wasn't wrong, for his car. The advice is just out of date."

That was the part that sat with him through the next two laps. His grandfather had not been wrong, exactly. He had been right about a world that had ended without notifying him. Alexis thought of the drawer at home full of maps nobody unfolded, the phone number still written inside the cover of an address book, and felt the strange vertigo of realizing you could inherit an injunction in perfect faith and perfect error at once. He said none of this out loud. He merely drove, and stopped, and steered.

At the end of the lesson she had him park beside a glacial ridge of plowed snow at the lot's edge, banked there since some earlier winter of the year. He shut off the engine and sat with his hands still on the wheel.

"That was decent," she said. "Book your next one at the desk."

In the waiting room, thawing, he found his grandfather leaning against the vending machine with the patience of a man who had been certain the lesson would end in a crash and was quietly relieved to be wrong. "How was it? Did you remember what I told you?"

"I stopped at a fence," Alexis said. "Pumping."

His grandfather expostulated, hands rising, the whole story of 1974 already assembling itself, wet mountain road, a station wagon, his father's arm across his chest in place of a seatbelt. Alexis listened to the end of it, then held up the keys he had been given and would have to return.

"The car has anti-lock brakes," he said. "You press and hold. You can still steer."

His grandfather looked at the keys, then at him, and for a moment said nothing at all, which from him was almost a concession. "Steer while braking," he repeated, slowly, testing the idea for cracks.

"That's what she said."

They walked out to the parking lot together, the old man a half step ahead, and Alexis watched him unlock his own car, pump the gas twice out of forty years of habit, and turn the key.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: French economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' argued that good economics must count the effects nobody sees.
story:
Sierra had made her decision already, which was why she could sit in Mr. Patel's office so calmly, arms folded, watching him shuffle the two envelopes on his desk as though they were still equal. One was the full scholarship to the state school forty minutes from her house. The other was the acceptance to the program in Montreal, no money attached, a French lit department her mother called impractical and her father called expensive. "I'm going to the state school," she said. "It's obvious. It's been obvious for weeks." She said it the way she said most things she was sure of, quickly, before anyone could examine it.

Mr. Patel was the guidance counsellor, a patient man with a peevish little clock on his desk that ticked a half-second behind the one on the wall, so the office always sounded slightly out of agreement with itself. "Okay," he said. "Then sign the intent form and we're done, and I'll be the first to congratulate you." He slid the form across. Sierra looked at the signature line and did not pick up the pen.

The night before, she had been at the coffee shop on Delancey with Trey, who was taking an economics elective second semester, and she had picked up his syllabus mainly to have something to do with her hands. Halfway down the reading list she saw an essay title that stopped her: "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen." She asked him what it meant, because it sounded like a fortune cookie pretending to be homework. "It's by this French economist, Frédéric Bastiat," Trey said. "From 1850. He argued that good economics has to count the effects nobody sees." She'd said something dismissive, she remembered, something about dead white men and broken windows, and Trey had laughed and taken the syllabus back, and she had spent the rest of the evening pretending to text people.

But the phrase had followed her home, had ridden in the car with her mother the next morning, had sat with her now in the ticking office. What was seen: the tuition number, zero dollars, her mother's face at the kitchen table going soft with relief, the word "free." What was not seen was harder, because it was, by definition, not seen. She could not put a number on the apartment in Montreal she would never rent, the seminar in translation she would never take, the version of herself who lived four hundred miles from everyone who had ever told her who she was.

"It's not that I don't know what I'm giving up," she said to Mr. Patel, which was not true, because until this week she had not let herself itemize it. "It's that giving it up is the responsible thing. Right? People say that. My mom's whole thing is, you don't turn down free money." Her mother had repeated the maxim so often over the years that Sierra had become inured to it, the way you get used to a smoke detector with a dying battery, a sound you register without hearing. Free money. Nobody ever asked what the money cost.

Mr. Patel leaned back. "I can't tell you which one, Sierra. You know that, right? I got in trouble my first year here for telling a girl which college to pick." He smiled at the clock, or past it. "But I can tell you the form isn't due until Friday, and you've said 'it's obvious' four times since you sat down, and obvious things usually only need saying once."

She wanted to argue with him, and found she could not, and the failure to argue felt like a door swinging open. Here were the two ways of thinking she had been carrying around like coins in the same pocket: her mother's arithmetic, where you counted what you could see, the numbers on the page, the debt that didn't exist, the graduation without loans; and Bastiat's harder ledger, where you also counted the invisible, the life not lived, the French she wouldn't speak, the distance she wouldn't cross. For years she had treated the second way of counting as self-indulgence, the trick you used to make bad decisions sound noble. Sitting in the misaligned tick of that office, she understood that it wasn't a trick, it was just accounting done honestly, and that both ledgers were true at once, and that no amount of cleverness would make them agree.

"Say I pick Montreal," she said slowly. "Then the thing I don't get is free tuition, and my mom works three more years like she's working now. Say I pick the state school. Then the thing I don't get is..." She stopped, because naming it out loud felt superstitious, like the naming would make it real. "Everything else, I guess. Or a lot of everything else."

"That sounds about right," Mr. Patel said. "Nobody's found a third envelope yet."

She signed the form on Thursday night, at the kitchen table, with her mother watching from the stove. The state school. She had built the decision carefully over three days, and it held, mostly, the way a patched tire holds: functional, honest about its seams. She would take French as her language requirement, she told her mother, and maybe a semester abroad, junior year, if the money was there, and the money might be there, and Montreal would still exist. Her mother hugged her, and the hug smelled like onions and relief, and Sierra held on longer than she needed to.

She went back to the coffee shop on Saturday to tell Trey, and found him at the corner table with the Bastiat essay actually printed out, pages marked in green highlighter, and she sat down across from him without asking. "I read the first two pages," he said. "It's about a broken window." She picked it up. "Start from the beginning," she said.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
The writing club met in the library's back corner, where the tables had initials carved into them by students who had presumably finished their papers before Stella ever started hers. She laid Mr. Baptiste's returned essay on the table like evidence at a trial. At the top, in green ink that was almost too cheerful for the news it carried, he had written: "Wrong system. Come see me." Her fourteen footnotes sat beneath the essay in tidy rows, each one apparently a crime.

"What system did you use?" Makena asked, sliding into the chair across from her and stealing a gummy worm from Stella's pencil case, which had become a shared resource some weeks ago without anyone announcing it.

"Chicago," Stella said. "Obviously. I did all of it. Superscripts, everything."

Nikolai leaned over from the next table, where he was supposed to be outlining a persuasive piece about vending machines. "Chicago has two systems," he said, with the restrained glee of someone who has waited all day to deploy a fact. "Notes and bibliography, and author-date."

"Well, nobody told the footnotes that," Stella said, but she said it quietly, because the sentence had landed somewhere. She remembered, in a small cold flash, the afternoon in the school library two weeks earlier, when she had found the style guide on the shelf and opened it to the middle instead of the front. There had been two different-looking sections. She had assumed one was an example and the other a variation, the way her grandmother had two recipes for the same cake and served whichever she felt like. She had copied the footnotes from the first section she landed on and never looked back.

Mr. Baptiste was shelving books near the window, because the writing club was technically supervised, though mostly he drank coffee and read the sports section. Stella carried the paper over. "I used footnotes," she said. "Is that not the point of Chicago?"

He glanced at her notes, then at her, and seemed to decide something. "Notes and bibliography is the one common in history and the humanities," he said. "Author-date is common in the sciences. You used the second one, at least partly. Your notes page has parenthetical citations and a reference list." He handed the paper back. "It's a fine paper, Stella. The argument's good. The machinery is from the wrong building."

"So I'm not wrong, I'm just wrong for the neighborhood," she said.

"Something like that," he said, and returned to his shelving, which he did with the air of a man pontificating through the medium of book spines.

Back at the table, Makena had arranged the gummy worms into a small audience. "Okay, so it's like this," Makena said. "You wrote a history paper wearing a lab coat."

"Which some people would call interdisciplinary," Nikolai offered, "and which Mr. Baptiste calls a seventy-eight."

Stella laughed despite herself. She pulled the style guide out of her bag, the same blue copy from the flashback of her own carelessness, and this time opened it to the front. She read the table of contents properly, like a person who had learned something, and found the two systems laid out side by side. Notes and bibliography for history and the humanities. Author-date for the sciences. She had assembled her paper out of both, a chimera with footnotes on one end and parenthetical citations on the other, and it had walked and breathed and received a grade.

Here was the part she hadn't expected: she liked the sciences version. The parenthetical dates told a reader instantly how recent a source was, which struck her as honest, even friendly. But the footnotes let her whisper asides, and asides were where she kept her best ideas, half-buried, the way she actually thought. She wasn't sure yet which she'd choose if the choice were ever hers, and the uncertainty felt less like failure than like standing in a doorway between two rooms, both lit.

She spent the rest of the meeting rebuilding the notes page, converting each parenthetical citation into a footnote, giggling at one of them, which cited a historian whose first name was Egbert. Makena read it aloud twice. When the bell for the late bus rang, Stella packed up slowly, then took the essay back to Mr. Baptiste at the window.

"Can I fix it and bring it Thursday?" she asked. "Also, if I ever write something that's sort of history and sort of science, which do I use?"

Mr. Baptiste considered the question longer than she expected, then tapped the cover of the style guide in her arms. "Ask whoever's grading it," he said. "Then ask yourself."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
story:
Luke had written the same opening line four times, and four times he had crossed it out, so the page in front of him looked like a fence that had lost an argument with a lawnmower. Ms. Ricci had assigned the class a ten-minute play drawn from a real moment in their own lives, and Luke's moment kept squirming away from him. It was the night his father's van broke down on the interstate and the two of them sat on the tailgate for three hours waiting for a tow truck, and it had felt enormous at the time, but on paper it kept turning into two guys saying nothing.

"You could just make stuff up," Crosby offered from the next desk. "Put in a sword fight. A mild one."

"I want it to be true," Luke said, and immediately wondered if that was even possible, since every time he remembered the tailgate, the headlights behind them got brighter than they had been, and his father's one good joke got funnier.

Ms. Ricci, overhearing, dropped a battered paperback on Luke's desk. Its spine was held together with tape that had itself been repaired with newer tape. "Read the production notes," she said, and walked off before it could feel like an assignment, which was her particular gift.

The book was The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, and there in the notes was Tennessee Williams calling it a memory play. Luke read the phrase twice. Then he read the first scene, where a man named Tom stepped out from the action and spoke straight to the audience, looking back on his family, telling them what he remembered and admitting it was memory, not fact. Luke put the book down and stared at the ceiling tiles as though they might congratulate him.

"Found something?" said Carys, leaning over from the third desk in the row, where she was attempting to resuscitate her own script, a comedy about a disastrous family dinner that had died somewhere around page two.

"It's called a memory play," Luke said. "The narrator gets to step out and just talk to the audience. He's remembering his family, so he can be honest that he's probably getting it wrong."

Carys considered this with the gravity of someone weighing a legal precedent. "So your play could have two of you. The you on the tailgate, and the you now, standing off to the side, telling us what it felt like."

"And admitting which parts he's embellishing," Luke said. "The narrator can literally interrupt himself." He was already writing, and the line that had refused to come arrived at a dead sprint: the older Luke steps forward, the stage goes dim, and he says that his father's joke about the tow truck driver was, in retrospect, medium at best, but that memory is ductile stuff, it bends toward whatever you need it to hold.

By Thursday the class was staging readings in the black box theatre, folding chairs in a horseshoe, and Luke had cast himself as the narrator and Crosby as his father, mostly because Crosby could do a devastating impression of an exhausted grown man. The moment came where the stage lights dropped to a single pool and Luke stepped out of the tailgate scene and told the audience, quietly, that he had made the headlights brighter. That in real life they had been ordinary, and he had spent two years polishing them into something cinematic, and he did not know why.

Afterward, in the corridor, Crosby clapped him on the shoulder. "Your dad's going to see this and sue you for defamation."

"He can't. It's theatre, not jurisprudence," Luke said, and Crosby laughed so hard at the word that a freshman actually turned around to see what was wrong with him.

Ms. Ricci caught Luke at the door. She said the narrator's confession was the strongest thirty seconds of the afternoon, and that the ending still bothered her, the way it stopped instead of landing. Luke said he knew. He had written three endings: one where the tow truck arrives, one where it doesn't, and one where the older Luke admits he has no idea how to end it because he still doesn't know what the night meant. He had chosen the third, and he wasn't sure that was courage or just an accurate report.

That night his father read the script at the kitchen table while pretending to watch the game. He got to the part about the joke being medium, and looked up.

"It was a good joke," his father said.

"It was fine," Luke said.

His father slid the script back across the table and tapped the last page. "Do the ending where you don't know," he said, and went back to the game, and Luke sat there holding the pages, the tape on the borrowed Menagerie visible in his bag beside them, and began, slowly, to grin.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The festival ran three blocks down Marrow Street, and the Seder table had been set up under a rented canopy between the falafel stand and the booth selling candles shaped like pomegranates. Keira carried a crate of grape juice toward the table, past her mother, who was arguing with the man from the rental company about folding chairs. Her mother had abrogated Keira's original job of watching the parking lot for the rabbi's car, which meant Keira was now free labor, and free labor gravitated toward crates.

Cassandra was already there, sitting sideways on a chair with a paperback Haggadah open on her knee. Cassandra was seventeen, a grade 12 student, and she had appointed herself coach for the evening because, as she put it, somebody had to. In front of her stood the youngest child at the table, a boy of six whose name Keira could never remember, holding his own Haggadah with both hands the way you hold a live animal.

"Again," Cassandra said. "From the top."

"Why is this night," the boy said, and stopped. He looked at the tablecloth.

"Breathe first. Then the whole line."

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Keira set the crate down. She knew the custom existed but had never watched it assembled in real time, never seen a big cousin bent over a small one, coaxing the words out one syllable at a time. In their family the youngest had always been somebody else, in somebody else's house. This year the youngest was here, and so the job was his, and the job was these questions.

The boy got through the first question and lost his nerve at the second. His chin dropped toward his chest and he became obdurate, declaring that he would not say it, that he had never said it, that a person could not be made to say things. Cassandra did not argue. She turned the Haggadah toward him and put her finger under the first word of the next question and left it there, resting, patient, while the festival went on around them. Somewhere behind the canopy a band tuned up, badly.

Keira's mother arrived with the apportionment chart, a laminated sheet that divided the catered food among forty-two seats, and began counting places with a pencil. Ms. Augustin, who lived two floors above Keira's family and had come down because the festival was on her street and because she was curious, stood at the end of the table and watched the boy. "Is he the one who sings?" she asked Keira, quietly.

"He asks," Keira said. "The youngest one asks the Four Questions. From the Haggadah. It starts with why is this night different from all other nights." She had heard it every year of her life and had never once had to describe it out loud to someone standing outside it, and the describing made her hear it fresh, as if the words had been waiting in her mouth with nothing to do until now.

"Why the youngest?" Ms. Augustin asked.

Keira started to answer and found she did not have one. She knew that it was the custom, and she knew the words, and she knew that at some point she had been the youngest, though she could not remember being coached, could not remember Cassandra's patience aimed at her. Maybe someone had done this for her and she had simply absorbed it the way you absorb a language, without the lesson ever surfacing. She said, honestly, "I don't know why. I just know that's how it goes."

Ms. Augustin nodded as though this were a sufficient answer, and perhaps it was, because meanwhile the boy had lifted his chin and begun again, unprompted, in a voice that started too loud and then steadied. "Why is this night different from all other nights?" He kept going, the second question, the third, his finger traveling under the lines while Cassandra's finger stayed half an inch ahead of his, both of them moving down the page together. Keira's mother stopped counting chairs. The band had stopped tuning. When he reached the end of the fourth question, Cassandra closed the Haggadah and put her hand flat on the cover, and the boy looked up at the whole table, waiting to find out what he had earned.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A buffer in GIS draws a zone of a set distance around a feature, such as every area within 100 meters of a river.
story:
The library's computer lab smelled of carpet glue and old radiators, and Brooklyn had claimed the terminal by the window because it was the only one where the screen didn't glare. Ms. Visser had shown her the basics of the geographic information system two Saturdays ago and then retreated behind the reference desk, on the theory, apparently, that sixteen-year-olds learn software the way they learn bruises. Brooklyn had spent an interminable first hour failing to import a shapefile, and then, without anything changing, it had worked.

The project was supposed to be simple. Her civics class wanted a map of the official flood zone on the east side, and the official flood zone, when she finally got it to render, was a modest blue splash along the river, tidy as a bruise itself. She overlaid the parcel data and the housing stock next, because Ms. Visver had said something in passing about how a map that shows only risk tells you who drowns, not who gets paid, and Brooklyn had written that down even though she wasn't sure she believed it.

"Is that the river?" Julianne had interposed herself over Brooklyn's shoulder, eating sunflower seeds she was not supposed to have in the lab. The shells were going into her hoodie pocket, a detail Brooklyn chose not to supervise.

"That's the flood zone," Brooklyn said. "The river's under it. Look, though." She pointed at the eastern edge, where the blue stopped in a clean line and a whole grid of houses continued past it, small rectangles marching toward the water. "The apartments Arman lives in, the brick ones, they're outside the zone. No flood insurance required, nothing. But they're close. Like, actually close."

Julianne leaned in, which did not improve her depth perception. "So make a buffer," she said, and when Brooklyn looked blank, she tapped the toolbar. "A buffer draws a zone of a set distance around a feature. Every area within a hundred meters of the river, if you set it to a hundred meters."

Brooklyn set it to a hundred meters. The map produced a second, wider band of color, and the grid of rectangles that had been safely outside the flood zone sat inside the new one the way passengers sit inside a bus, most of them not even knowing they'd boarded. Arman's building was in it. So was the laundromat, the halal grocery, and a stretch of Mill Street she'd walked a hundred times without thinking of it as near anything.

She printed it, because Ms. Visser liked paper and because Brooklyn liked the small ceremony of it, the map sliding warm out of the tray. On the printout she could see what the screen had only implied: within the buffer, the housing was almost entirely rentals, and outside it, past the tracks, the parcels grew lawns. She didn't write a conclusion on it. She was honest enough with herself to know the buffer was a choice, a hundred meters instead of eighty or a hundred and fifty, and that a more generous line would have caught different houses, and that she couldn't say why a hundred was the right number except that it was round.

Arman came by after his shift at the grocery, still smelling faintly of cumin, and stood over the printout with his hands in his apron pocket. "That's my building," he said, not alarmed, just noting it, the way you note your own name in a list of strangers. He traced the band with one finger, then the official flood line, then back. "So we're not in the flood zone."

"No," Brooklyn said. "You're in mine."

Ms. Visser passed behind them on her way to shelve returns, glanced at the map, and paused. She looked at it longer than a librarian looks at a student project. "Interesting," she said, which was the most she ever said. Then, almost as an afterthought: "The county did one of these two years ago. Internal, never published." She set her cart down. "They used the same distance."

Brooklyn asked how she knew, and Ms. Visser only smiled the way people smile when the answer would take longer than the question deserved, and rolled the cart on toward the 300s. Arman picked up the printout, folded it once, and put it inside his apron, over his heart like a letter he'd been waiting for.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest.
story:
The history museum's Cold War gallery smelled like floor wax and old radiator, and Alexander had commandeered the bench nearest the big wall map before Angelo could claim it. He sat with two photocopies on his knee, one from a historian named Willis who said the United States had built the Cold War out of economic ambition, and one from a historian named Feaver who said the Soviets had built it out of paranoia and control. His essay was due Monday. Ms. Kaur had written one word in the margin of his draft, and the word was "Evidence?"

"That map," Angelo said, pointing with a pretzel he wasn't supposed to have in the gallery. "Why is half of Europe blank?"

Alexander looked up. The map showed the Marshall Plan countries shaded in blue, a solid band across the west, and then a clean pale nothing from the Baltic down through the middle of the continent. He had walked past it twice without seeing it. "I don't know," he said, which felt like a dangerous thing to say out loud here, since the whole point of the trip was that they were supposed to know things.

Amine drifted over from the display case of ration books, reading a panel aloud in the low voice of someone performing boredom. "It says the aid was offered to Europe, all of it. So why is Czechoslovakia blank? They're not even next to Russia."

Alexander stood, essay forgotten, and walked the map's edge like a man checking a fence. He found the small print underneath. The aid had been offered broadly; the Soviet Union had refused it for itself; and it had pressed the Eastern European governments, Czechoslovakia among them, to withdraw their applications, even though Czechoslovakia had first shown real interest in taking part. He read the line twice. The blue shading suddenly looked less like a wall the Americans had built and more like a shape made by two hands pressing from both sides, and he could not tell yet which hand had pressed harder.

"Okay," Amine said, watching him. "You have the face. The essay face."

"Willis says the Americans designed the plan to divide Europe," Alexander said slowly. "Feaver says the Soviets turned it into a division. And this," he tapped the glass, "this is a thing that actually happened, that both of them have to explain. Czechoslovakia wanted in. Moscow made them pull out." He was talking faster now, the way he did when he was thinking out loud and couldn't stop. "So Willis has to say the U.S. knew Moscow would do that, that the offer was bait. Which maybe. But Feaver has to say the plan was innocent, which is also maybe, because of course a country giving away that much money wants something back."

Angelo offered him a piece of pretzel, which Alexander took without noticing he'd done it. "So write that they're both wrong," Angelo said. "Boom. Essay done. Let's get lunch."

"It's not that they're both wrong. It's that the fact fits both of them." Alexander sat back down on the bench, elbows on knees. "The withdrawal happened. That's solid. What it means is the argument. Feaver can point at Moscow ordering Prague around; Willis can point at Washington knowing Moscow would order Prague around. The map doesn't tell you which story is true. It just tells you the map isn't the whole map."

Ms. Kaur appeared behind them with the unhurried timing of someone who had been listening for ten minutes. She was carrying the clipboard she used to count heads, and she counted theirs, and then she didn't leave. "Find something?" she asked.

"He found a crisis," Amine said. "A personal one."

"Half of one," Alexander said. He showed her the two photocopies, then the map, and explained the problem the way you explain a splinter you can't reach: carefully, hoping someone else's fingers are better angled than yours. "I can't decide which historian the evidence favors, and I'm starting to think that's the honest answer, and I hate it, because 'I can't decide' sounds like I didn't do the work."

Ms. Kaur looked at the blank half of the map for a moment. "Or it sounds like you did," she said. "There's a museum coffee machine that takes exact change and dispenses something the brochure would call cocoa. Amine, you look indigent. I'm buying." She fished coins out of her jacket, and when Amine protested that he had money, she said restitution could take the form of him carrying the clipboard for the rest of the afternoon, and he took it from her with mock ceremony, like a squire accepting a sword.

Alexander stayed on the bench a minute longer, copying the small print into his notebook word for word, because the fact was the one thing in the room he was sure of. Angelo leaned over his shoulder and read it upside down. "Czechoslovakia really wanted the money?"

"Really wanted the money."

"Poor blank countries," Angelo said, and shaded in Czechoslovakia on the map's reflection in the display glass with the side of his fist, smudging it lightly with a pretzel crumb.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
story:
The phone store smelled like floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Alexandre had been standing at the display case for eleven minutes when the sales clerk finally came over. Behind the glass, the model he wanted sat with its screen lit, showing a photograph of a lake so blue it looked invented. It cost more than he had, and more than he would have by September, unless he did something about the plan Joey had proposed on Tuesday.

"Three names on one contract," Joey had said, leaning across the cafeteria table. "Hannah, me, you. Split the bill three ways, everybody gets unlimited data, nobody pays full price. Hannah's already in." Hannah had nodded, but slowly, the way she nodded when she was reserving judgment, and Alexandre had said maybe, which he'd learned from his mother meant no until further notice.

The clerk was a young woman with a lanyard and a tablet. "You're eighteen?" she asked, and Alexandre said sixteen, and she said he'd need an adult on the account, a co-signer, someone whose credit could be checked, and his stomach dropped the way it did when a door closed somewhere in the house and he knew it was his father home early. His mother worked until six. His father answered phones all day and came home sullen and monosyllabic, and the last thing Alexandre wanted was to hand him a contract to sign at dinner.

"Unless," the clerk said, scrolling, "you've got somebody over eighteen who wants to be on it with you. Then it's a joint account."

Joey had a brother, but the brother was a reactionary about phones, about screens, about most things, and called them surveillance devices, so that was out. Hannah turned eighteen in October. Alexandre himself turned seventeen in November. It was June, and the phone behind the glass was on a summer promotion that ended Sunday.

"Can my friend be on it?" he asked. "She's eighteen in four months."

The clerk's mouth did something polite. "She'd have to be eighteen now. Or your parent signs, and your friends can be authorized users. They get lines on the account." She swiped to a new screen. "But if you're thinking of putting more than one adult on the contract, you should read this part." She turned the tablet toward him and pointed to a paragraph under the heading marked Liability.

He read it twice. Under joint and several liability, each person who signed could be held responsible for the entire amount, not just their own share. If Joey stopped paying his third, the company didn't chase Joey. It could chase whoever had the money, or the patience, or the fear of collections, and that person would owe the whole bill, all of it, and would have to recover Joey's part from Joey on his own.

"You look like you found something," the clerk said.

"If my name's on it with somebody else, I could owe all of it? Not just my part?"

"That's what joint and several means," she said. "Whole amount. Some people like it because it keeps everybody honest. Some people don't like it for the same reason."

Alexandre thought of Joey, who had borrowed twenty dollars in March and repaid it in coins over six weeks, and who was generous and warm and genuinely meant everything he promised at the moment he promised it. He thought of Hannah, who kept a spreadsheet of who owed what and texted reminders on Sundays. Joey would pay, probably, eventually, and the word probably sat in Alexandre's chest like a stone with sharp edges. He did not want to spend the year being Hannah's collection agency, and he did not want to spend it being Joey's creditor either, tallying weeks, sending texts that curdled a friendship into accounting.

"Can I see the full terms?" he asked, and the clerk printed them, eleven pages, and he stood near the accessories wall and read the sections on cancellation, on consent, on what happened when a payment failed. The print was small and the language wanted to be unread, but he worked through it. At one point a toddler by the repair counter dropped a phone box and began to cry, and the fluorescent light seemed to transfigure the whole aisle into something colder and brighter than a store ought to be, and he kept reading anyway.

When he was done, he brought the pages back. "One more question. If my mom signs, and it's just her name on the contract, and Joey and Hannah are users on my line. Then she owes it all if we mess up?"

"That's how it works, yeah."

"But she knows that going in. It's her decision, not mine deciding for her." He heard how it sounded, like he was arguing with himself out loud, and maybe he was. Joey would call this backing out. Joey would say, you're not the guy who reads eleven pages, and Alexandre would have to say, I am now, apparently.

He called his mother at work. She answered on the fourth ring, her voice low the way it went when she was between meetings. He explained the plan, the shared cost, the clause, the whole-amount part, and the fact that if Joey missed a month it would land on her, not on him.

"Read me that part again," she said. He read it. There was a pause with typing in it.

"I'll look at the papers tonight," she said. "If I sign, you three sort out your own shares before the month starts, not after. And Joey pays on the first. Not when he gets around to it."

"He'll say yes," Alexandre said. "Saying yes isn't his problem."

"I know what his problem is," she said. "I'll see the papers tonight."

He hung up and gave his name and number to the clerk, who put the phone on hold for him at the promotional price until Monday. He folded the eleven pages into quarters and put them in his back pocket, and on his way out he stopped at the display case once more. The screen had gone dark, and his reflection stood there holding the folded contract, and he lifted his hand toward the glass and pressed one finger against the cold surface, just below the price.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners.
story:
The resolution on the whiteboard read: This house believes a company's only duty is to its shareholders. Gabrielle was arguing the affirmative, which she had chosen in September partly because she believed it and partly because Mr. Hassan had said the affirmative case rewarded discipline. She believed it less now, in the third round of regionals, but she had learned not to let that show.

Her case ran clean. Profits, she said, were not greed but a promise kept; the people who bought shares had lent the company their savings, and a manager who spent those savings on anything else was spending money that was not hers to spend. She used the phrase "fiduciary duty" three times and watched two judges nod on the third. The room was spartan, a borrowed classroom with the desks pushed into a horseshoe, and the radiator ticked like a slow metronome under the windows.

Then Ashlee stood for the negative, and instead of the emotional appeal Gabrielle had prepped against, Ashlee pulled out a book, held it up so the judges could see the faded cover, and read the year aloud. Nineteen eighty-four. "R. Edward Freeman, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach," she said. "He argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners. Workers. Suppliers. The town." She set the book down on the desk with a small, deliberate click. "Not because it's nice. Because the bus driver and the payroll clerk and the river all have a claim, and a manager who pretends otherwise is just choosing whose claims to ignore."

In cross-examination, Gabrielle tried the line she'd rehearsed: "If everyone's responsible to everyone, isn't no one responsible to anyone?" It sounded better at two in the morning in Jane's kitchen. Ashlee didn't flinch. "Or it means responsibility is bigger than one ledger line," she said. "Which of us is avoiding responsibility, exactly?" The second judge wrote something long.

During the break, Jane found her in the hallway by the water fountain. Jane had come to hold notes and had ended up holding nothing, since Gabrielle preferred index cards to paper. "You're going to lose the round," Jane said, not unkindly. Gabrielle said she knew that. What she didn't say, and what she suspected Jane knew anyway, was that losing had begun to feel less like the point than like a door.

Because the night before, at her job at the grocery store, the manager had taped a new schedule to the break-room corkboard. Closing shift moved from nine to eleven, which suited the store, since the district wanted later hours for the holiday rush. But Tomas, who stocked dairy and took the 9:40 bus, stood in front of the board for a long time, then said quietly that the last bus left at 10:15 and a cab was eighteen dollars each way, and that the change would cost him more per week than it paid him. The manager said he'd see what he could do, in the tone of a man closing a drawer. Nobody undulates around a corkboard, but the whole break room had rippled with that particular silence, everyone deciding not to be the next one to speak.

Gabrielle had thought about it all night, and now, with two minutes left before her rebuttal, she thought about it again. Freeman's word was stakeholder, and she tested it against what she'd seen: the store had treated Tomas as a cost, as someone outside the decision, when in fact the decision was made almost entirely inside his life. That was the trade-off nobody had written down. The unintended consequence was printed on the bus schedule.

When her rebuttal came, she gave the judges the strongest version of the shareholders' case she could, because that was her job and she had said she would do it. Then, with forty seconds left, she set her index cards face down on the desk. "I want to concede something," she said. "My side treats one set of claims as real and the rest as charity. But I watched a schedule change this week that helped a store and quietly took money out of a worker's pocket, and no one broke a rule. So my position, honestly held, is this: the shareholder model tells the truth about a promise, and the stakeholder model tells the truth about a blast radius, and I don't yet know how to hold both." She sat down. The radiator ticked. Ashlee was looking at her with something that had stopped being competitive.

Mr. Hassan found her afterward while the judges conferred in the empty library. "That last bit," he said. "It cost you the round, probably." He waited, and she let the silence stand, because she suspected he wanted her to regret it and she didn't. "It might have won you the next four years," he said finally, and walked off toward the vending machine.

Ashlee came over holding the Freeman book, arms crossed over it like a shield. "I actually skimmed it at a used bookstore last summer because my mom made me," she said. "Half of it is about managers, not morals. It's kind of boring, honestly." Gabrielle laughed, the first real laugh of the day. "Can I borrow it anyway?" Ashlee looked at the book, then at the horseshoe of desks where the judges would soon return with a verdict neither of them would much care about, and held it out. "Bring it back Monday," she said. "And underline better than I did."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The chemistry lab was subterranean, half below the courtyard, so the windows started at ankle height and showed only the shoes of students crossing to the portables. Alexa liked it down there anyway. Nothing came in except what you brought with you, and today she had brought two cups of coffee she wasn't allowed to have and a prediction sheet she couldn't finish.

The sheet asked one question. In the beaker at the front bench, a pale solution sat in equilibrium, and Ms. Katz was going to lower it into a hot water bath in front of everyone. Before the demo, each of them had to write which way the equilibrium would shift when it warmed, toward the reactants or toward the products, and say why. Alexa had stared at her answer line so long the graphite had gone shiny.

"Toward the reactants," Maiya said, leaning across the aisle. "Heat is like a product, right? You add product, it shifts back the other way. Everyone knows that."

"Everyone except the textbook," Montana said. She was a stoic about most things, storms, lost games, her own birthday, but she leaned forward now. "That rule is for when the reaction gives off heat. This one takes it in. It's not the same situation."

"It's heat either way."

"It's not the same direction of heat."

Ms. Katz walked past with the water bath, steaming, and set it on the front bench beside the beaker of pale solution. "Ten more minutes," she said, and did not look at anyone's paper. She never looked at anyone's paper before a prediction, which Alexa had always respected and today found unbearable.

Alexa tried Maiya's way first, because Maiya's way had a music to it. Add something to one side, the balance swings the other way, everything settles again, tidy as a scale. But the sentence on the sheet said the forward reaction absorbed heat, took it in, and that snagged her. She thought about her own hands in February, how they stayed cold even indoors, how cold was a thing you could hold onto. If the forward direction was a thing that swallowed heat, then heat was what it ate. You feed it and you feed the thing that eats. She wrote nothing yet, but she turned her pencil over and erased her half-formed answer, the one she'd copied toward the reactants, the one Maiya was still defending two rows away in a furious whisper.

"I'm telling you, I got this exact question right on the practice quiz," Maiya said.

"On a different reaction," Montana said.

"You don't know that."

"Then neither do you."

Alexa looked at the beaker. Pale, patient, stoic as anything in the room, giving away nothing about which way it would go. That was the part that beguiled her, honestly, that a liquid could sit there holding two futures at once and show you only the one it had. She thought again about Maiya's rule and Montana's objection and understood, finally, that they weren't really disagreeing about the rule. They were disagreeing about whether this reaction faced one way or the other, and the sheet had already told her. Forward takes in heat. She wrote: if the forward reaction absorbs heat, then raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. Her hand hovered. She could still be wrong. The whole point of a prediction was that it could shame you.

"Time," Ms. Katz said. "Pencils down. Don't change anything, and don't tell me it doesn't count if you whisper it after."

The beaker went into the bath. For a moment nothing happened, and the room went quiet in a way it hadn't been all period, thirty people not breathing at a liquid. The suspense stretched. Alexa watched the surface of the solution, pale and still, and felt her own answer sitting on her paper like a wager.

Then the color began to change, climbing up from the bottom of the beaker where the warmth touched it first, deepening shade by shade, unmistakable, and Maiya made a small wounded sound, and Montana put both palms flat on the table without a word. The color was the products' color. Ms. Katz lifted the beaker out, held it to the subterranean window light, and said, "Now, the cold bath. Before I put it in, write your next prediction."

Alexa was already writing.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The hit came in the eighteenth minute, a shoulder Michael never saw, and the turf came up to meet him in a way that suggested the ground had been waiting all afternoon for its chance. He lay there while the whistle shrilled above him. The sky assembled itself in pieces, then all at once, and Mr. Kelly was crouching beside him before Michael had finished deciding whether the grass smelled like grass or like something else.

"Look at me," Mr. Kelly said. "Follow my finger."

Michael followed the finger. It was not difficult. He felt fine, which he said, twice, while the trainer helped him sit up and the game resumed twenty metres away without him. From the sideline he watched Makai take his position on the wing, watched Salma shouting orders from the back line, and the half unraveled slowly into a one-goal deficit that felt, from the bench, like something being stolen from him personally.

At halftime he stood in front of Mr. Kelly in the shade of the goal frame and made his case. He felt fine. His vision was clear. He had no headache, no nausea, nothing. He wanted to say it in writing, sign it, have it notarized; he'd swear an affidavit if that was what it took. Salma, towelling her hair, said that wasn't how any of this worked, and Mr. Kelly said something quiet that Michael did not want to hear.

"I'm not saying you're lying," Mr. Kelly said. "I'm saying the guideline doesn't care how you feel. A suspected concussion, you don't go back in the same day. Even if you feel fine."

"Suspected by who?"

"By me. That's the job they gave me."

Michael sat down on the cooler and malign nothing, though he wanted to. The referee had been bad all season, malevolent almost, in Michael's private accounting, and it was easier to be angry at the shoulder, the whistle, the whole architecture of the afternoon than to sit with what was actually happening, which was that his body had been assessed by someone other than himself and found, provisionally, untrustworthy. He had always assumed he was the final authority on his own head. The second half started without him.

Makai came off in the sixtieth minute with cramps and dropped onto the grass beside him, breathing hard. "You look fine," Makai said.

"I am fine."

"So why are you sitting here?"

Michael started to answer, then didn't. There was a version of the answer that made him sound wise and a version that made him sound defeated, and he wasn't sure yet which one was true. The sun had moved, and the half-shadow of the goalpost lay across his legs like a bar. On the field, Salma was arguing with the referee about a throw-in, her hands out, insistent, and Michael felt the peculiar ache of watching his team need someone and not being allowed to be that someone, for reasons that resided entirely inside his own skull and could not be argued with, or sworn away, or appealed.

They lost by two. In the parking lot afterward, his mother asked him questions the trainer had written on a folded sheet of paper, and he answered them all correctly, which proved something, though he no longer felt certain what. Mr. Kelly stopped by the car before leaving.

"You might be completely fine," he said. "Probably you are. Tomorrow you see the doctor and go from there." He put his clipboard under his arm. "You played well before it happened. That run in the tenth minute was the best thing anyone did all game."

Michael nodded. He believed him about the run, and he believed the guideline, and he understood that both of those things could be true at once, that the rule was right even if it was wrong about him, or might be wrong about him, which was the part no one could ever know for sure. He got in the car. Through the windshield the empty field lay flat and green under the lights, the goal at the far end still standing, the net rippling once in the wind and going still.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
The dentist's waiting room smelled like mint and carpet cleaner, and Arianna spread her flashcards across two chairs because there was no one else in the room except Aila, who was there for moral support, and a woman by the window reading a magazine with a cracked spine. Tomorrow morning, fourth period, Arianna had to stand in front of Ms. Rossi's health class and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections, a talk she had volunteered for and had been regretting since roughly the moment she raised her hand.

"Okay," she said, flipping the first card. "Consent. Say it back to me."

"Consent is when both people want it and say so, and either one can change their mind," Aila recited, then winced as the receptionist's door opened and a hygienist called a name that was not hers. "You could at least wait until we're somewhere private."

"That's the whole point. If I can't say it in a dentist's waiting room, I can't say it in front of thirty people, half of whom I've known since kindergarten." Arianna tapped the card. "The embarrassing part is the feature, not the bug."

Aila considered this. "That sounded pithy. Did you rehearse it?"

"I rehearsed it in the shower, yes."

The second card was harder. Contraception, and under it a list: pill, condom, implant, IUD, ring, patch, shot. Arianna knew the list; what she did not know was how to rank them, and Keira, who was apparently also due for a cleaning that afternoon, dropped into the chair beside Aila ten minutes later with a pamphlet she'd taken from a rack near the receptionist's desk. "They had a whole shelf of these," Keira said, "next to the floss. Read the middle part."

Arianna read it twice, lips moving. Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants failed in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, the pamphlet said, and then came the part that made her sit up straight: once placed by a clinician, they did not depend on daily use. She copied it onto a fresh card, then looked up. "Wait. So the pill fails more not because it's weaker, but because it's on you every single day?"

"Which is basically the story of my life," Keira said, "including but not limited to my water intake and my homework."

"That's the thing though." Arianna's pen stopped. "I was going to rank the methods like they're grades, best to worst. But it's not that. It's which one you can actually live with, day after day, without a single missed day. It's reliability in real life, not reliability in a lab." She wrote a note to herself in the margin: same person, different behavior, different outcome.

The hygienist called Keira back, which meant the remaining flashcards fell to Aila, who held them at arm's length like they might be contagious. The third section was the clinic talk: how to get tested, what to say when you call, what the visit is actually like. Aila read the first card silently and then said, "This bit where you wrote 'they won't tell your parents, ask about confidentiality when you book.' Is that true?"

"It's true for the clinic Ms. Rossi gave us the number for. You ask them directly. That's what the number is for."

"Good." Aila set the card down. "Because the way we learned it in middle school, you'd think going to a clinic meant something was wrong with you. Like the whole thing existed to pathologize you."

Arianna had not thought of it that way and now could not stop. She drew a line through the heading on her first card, "Being Safe," and stared at the blank space. The middle school version had made it all sound like damage control. But tomorrow's talk could be the opposite: ordinary, like a checkup, like the cleaning Keira was currently getting behind that door. Health, not danger. "I need a new title," she said.

"How about 'Nothing Has to Be Wrong to Ask a Question'?"

"That's long."

"It's honest," Aila said, "and after four years of 'just say no to everything,' I think we've earned long."

The receptionist looked over at them then, and Arianna braced for a shushing, but the woman only said, "You two want more pamphlets? We keep a box." She slid it across the counter, and Arianna saw the whole shelf of them, floss on one side, information on the other, waiting for anyone who walked in. She took six.

When Keira came back out, cheeks numb and talking sideways around the gauze, Arianna read her the first minute of the talk, stumbling only once, at the part where she explained that either person could stop at any time and that asking was not a mood-killer but the whole point. Keira listened, spat discreetly into a napkin, and said, "You're going to say 'utilize' at some point, aren't you."

"Use. I'll say use."

"Good, because the difference isn't just semantics, one of them makes you sound like a pamphlet."

Arianna laughed, gathered the cards, and squared them into her bag with the pamphlets underneath, the box still open on the counter behind her. She didn't know yet how the class would take it, whether they'd snicker at the word condom or go quiet, whether the boy in the second row who joked about everything would make it through. What she had was the order of the cards, the number for the clinic written large on the last one, and Aila already saying, "One more run-through before the bus."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
story:
Rebecca had taped the poster of Frida Kahlo to the clothesline with two clothespins and a strip of masking tape that kept surrendering in the heat, so the whole thing drooped like Kahlo herself was tired of being looked at. This was the problem. Ms. Kovalenko's assignment demanded formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, due Monday, and Rebecca had a backyard, a lemonade, and no ideas.

"You could just write that she looks sad," said Nadine, flopping into the deck chair with the gravity of someone offering real scholarship. "Sad is a theme."

"Sad is not a theme, it's a mood, and Ms. Kovalenko will feed it back to me shredded." Rebecca stood back from the poster, arms crossed, as though distance might organize the painting for her. In the image Kahlo stared out from a wall of leaves, a thorn necklace digging into her throat, and from the necklace hung a small dead hummingbird, wings spread, chest dulled. "The monkey's holding the thorns tighter. The cat's bored. There's a dragonfly, butterflies in her hair, and this bird, which honestly looks like a decoration somebody glued on."

"A lugubrious decoration," said Christophe, arriving over the fence the way he always did, one sneaker first. He considered himself the group's vocabulary. "That's my word for the week. It means gloomy, mournful, excessively sad. Perfect for a dead bird."

"It's not decoration," said Nadine, squinting. "Nothing in her stuff is just decoration. She's not that kind of painter. There's always consonance between things, like the thorns and the necklace, pain and jewellery saying the same thing twice."

"Consonance," Rebecca repeated, and pulled her notebook off the picnic table. She liked the word, and she liked Nadine's instinct, but instinct wasn't analysis. Ms. Kovalenko wanted colour relationships, compositional weight, symbolic function, and a considered position, which was teacher-language for "have an opinion and survive having it." The green behind Kahlo was a flat, deliberate green, the same green as the leaves, so the figure emerged from it and was trapped by it at once. The hummingbird sat at the exact centre, at the throat, where a voice would be. Rebecca wrote: centre, throat, voice, dead. Then she crossed out "dead" because it felt like showing off.

From the other side of the fence came the sound of a watering can, and then Ms. Kovalenko's head appeared above the tomatoes, reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She looked at the drooping poster for a long moment. "That bird," she said. "It's a Mexican folk charm. For luck in love."

Then she went back to her tomatoes, as though she had commented on the weather, and Rebecca stood very still. Christophe mouthed the word "charm" at Nadine. Nadine had already grabbed the notebook and was flipping to a blank page.

"So the dead bird is a love charm," Rebecca said slowly, writing it down. "A dead thing hung at the throat for luck in love. That's not lugubrious, Christophe, or, it's lugubrious and something else at the same time. It's ironic. She wears the hope of love like jewellery and it's a corpse." She looked at the poster again and the painting seemed to rearrange itself slightly, quietly, the way a sentence does when you find the verb. The thorns drew blood toward the charm. The monkey pulled them tighter. The butterflies, the dragonfly, the cat, all of them clustered around that one small dead centre like arguments around a thesis.

"Okay but is it luck or is it despair?" Nadine asked, chewing the pen cap. "Because you can't write 'it means both,' that's a cop-out."

"Why not? Maybe the honest position is that she's showing wanting love as something that costs blood and hope in the same breath, and I can't tell which side of it she's on." Rebecca paused. "Ms. Kovalenko said a considered position. She didn't say a resolved one."

Christophe stretched out on the grass with his hands behind his head. "Then write that. Say the composition holds two things at once, that the charm at the centre adumbrates the whole question, you know, hints at it without settling it. Then she thinks you did it on purpose, and you get an A instead of a shredded mood essay."

Rebecca looked at him, then at Nadine, then at the painting hanging crooked on the clothesline, one clothespin finally giving up so the corner curled toward the sky. She pinned it back, straightened it, and tapped the hummingbird once with her finger, gently, the way you'd touch something that was once alive.

"Luck in love," she said. "For your sake, I hope it works."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
story:
Ms. Wiśniewski stopped them at the switchback where the trail opened onto a granite shelf, and while the others drank water she unrolled a laminated map and weighted its corners with four pebbles, which struck Emily as an excessive number of pebbles for one map until the wind came up the slope and she understood. "Currents," Ms. Wiśniewski said. "Thursday's quiz will ask you to read one of these and tell me what it means for climate. So we practice here, where the wind will take the map if you don't pay attention, which is its own kind of lesson, I suppose." Emily crouched beside it, Jovan on her left, Vienna on her right, the three of them casting a shared shadow over the North Atlantic.

The map was mostly blue, veined with red and blue arrows that curved like handwriting she couldn't read. She had looked at these before, in the textbook, and seen only decoration. Now she tried to actually read them, the way you'd read a trail: an arrow meant movement, a direction, something carried from one place to another. A thick red line ran north along the American coast, hugging the shoreline like a freeway, and then, at a bump of land labeled Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, it did something strange. It let go. It swung away from the coast and bent northeast, straight out across the whole gray expanse of the Atlantic toward Europe.

"Why there?" Emily said, mostly to herself, tracing the bend with one finger, careful not to smudge the lamination she was already smudging.

"Why what, why does it leave?" Jovan leaned over her shoulder. "Maybe the coast just runs out of coast."

Vienna, who had a personal policy of disagreeing with Jovan approximately hourly, crouched down. "Coasts don't run out. Look, it goes northeast across the Atlantic. That's a decision. That's a current with a plan." She tapped Europe. "And it's red, so it's warm, so where's it taking all that warm water?"

Emily followed the arrow to its end and felt the small click of two ideas meeting. Warm water, carried from the coast of North America all the way across. Her mother had a friend in Dublin who grew roses in a garden at the same latitude as Newfoundland, where, her mother liked to say, the roses spent most of the year as an act of faith. She had never thought to ask why. She looked at the latitude lines, ran her finger along the parallels, and there it was: the arrow ended at Europe's northern edge. "It warms it," she said slowly. "The warm water leaves the US coast at Cape Hatteras and turns northeast across the Atlantic, and northern Europe is where it arrives. That's why Dublin isn't Newfoundland."

"That's the quiz answer," Jovan said, with something like awe. "You just got the quiz answer from roses."

"I'm not sure I did." Emily was already doubting it, the way she doubted a good idea on principle, to see whether it survived. The Gulf Stream, that was the name in the map's legend, in small serious capitals. But how much of the warmth was the water, and how much the wind riding above the water, she couldn't tell from arrows. The map showed what moved, not what it carried. She said as much, and Vienna made a skeptical noise.

"That's very you," Vienna said. "You find a whole answer and then interrogate it for fun."

"Some of it stays uncertain," Emily said. "That's allowed."

Ms. Wiśniewski had drifted closer at some point, and Emily felt a flicker of foreboding, the specific kind she got when a teacher had been listening and was about to say something incisive that she would think about for a week. But all Ms. Wiśniewski said was, "Hold the corner, it's lifting," and Emily pinned the map down with the heel of her hand while the wind tried again to take the Atlantic away.

Jovan pointed at another arrow, a blue one running south along Africa, and asked whether it went the other way, and Vienna began to argue that of course it did, everything went the other way somewhere, and Emily looked at the red line bending off Hatteras one more time. A current leaves home at a particular spot on a particular coast and crosses an ocean, and lands that never see it stay cold and lands that receive it grow roses, and the map doesn't tell you which part is the water's doing and which is the wind's, only that the warm arrow points northeast. She could live with that. She would write it Thursday, both halves, the answer and the not-knowing.

"Ready?" Ms. Wiśniewski rolled the map tight, pebbles scattered downhill, and Emily stood and shouldered her pack. Vienna was still explaining the African current to Jovan, who was acceding to it in the tone of a person surrendering a city, and the trail went on up through the pines. Emily took one last look east, past the trees, toward where the ocean would be, and followed.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
The rain had been going since second period, and the tall windows of the school library held it in long, trembling lines. Nevaeh spread her two articles across the table like cards she didn't trust: one by a researcher who claimed later school start times improved adolescent sleep, and one whose data showed almost no effect at all. Ms. Friedman's assignment sheet sat between them, folded once, its key sentence underlined twice. Compare the arguments, it said. Take a position. She had been at the table for forty minutes and had written one sentence, which she had then crossed out.

Aiyana dropped into the chair opposite her with a granola bar and no apparent agenda. "Still fighting with the sleep thing?"

"They're both so sure," Nevaeh said. She tapped the first article. "This one tracked four hundred students for a term. Grades up, car crashes down, everybody happy." She tapped the second. "This one says the change just made kids stay up later, so nothing improved. Four hundred students too. Different district, different numbers, opposite conclusions."

"Flip a coin," Aiyana said around a mouthful of oats.

"That's the problem. Ms. Friedman doesn't want a coin flip. She wants a considered position, whatever that means." Nevaeh looked at the rain again. Somewhere behind the reference desk, Finnegan was printing something, the printer shuddering through each page as if it resented the work. She thought about what her mother always said about arguments, that the loudest person in the room usually had the least to say. Both articles were loud. Maybe the answer was to find someone quiet, someone who hadn't run one study but had somehow looked at all of them.

She turned to the library's single row of dated computers and typed her question differently this time. Instead of arguing with either author, she searched for studies about the studies. The screen gave her a title she hadn't seen before, something with a word she had to sound out under her breath: meta-analysis. Finnegan drifted over, drawn by the word the way he was drawn by anything that sounded like a villain's plan.

"Is that a real thing or did you typo?"

"It's real," she said, reading. "A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can." She sat back. "So it's not another four hundred kids. It's all of them. Every study on start times, pooled." She said it again, slower, testing the weight of it. "More precise than any single study."

Finnegan leaned in. "So who wins?"

"That's the thing. It's not about winning." She found the pooled result halfway down the page, a small effect, real but modest, larger in some districts than others. Neither article had been lying; each had seen its own four hundred students truly. But each had also mistaken its corner for the whole room. She copied the citation into her notes, and the uncertainty that had been sitting on her chest all week didn't vanish so much as settle into a shape she could work with. She would argue for the modest effect, and she would be honest that the variation across districts was something she couldn't yet explain.

She wrote for an hour while Aiyana did chemistry flashcards and the rain thinned toward evening. Once she paused over the word endemic, deciding whether sleep deprivation deserved it, and decided it did: chronic, everywhere in the data, woven into adolescent life like a leitmotif that kept surfacing in every study she read. Around four o'clock, her third paragraph threatened to destabilize the whole essay by conceding too much to the second article, and she let it, then rebuilt the fourth paragraph on top of the concession rather than against it. That, she suspected, was what considered meant: not a fortress, but a structure that could hold its own doubts.

Ms. Friedman passed the table on her way to shelve returns and paused at the title of the meta-analysis on Nevaeh's screen. "That's a good instinct," she said, and moved on before it could become praise Nevaeh would have to live up to.

Aiyana packed up her flashcards, zipped her bag, and looked over Nevaeh's shoulder at the last line on the page. "Still not sure, though. Right?"

"Still not sure," Nevaeh said, and kept typing.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Seder, a piece of the middle matzah called the afikoman is set aside, often hidden for children to find, and eaten as the last food of the meal.
story:
The Haggadah lay open on the tablecloth before Edouard, its pages soft with antiquity, and across it his grandmother's finger tapped twice, the way she tapped when a silence had gone on long enough. Twelve people waited. The soup was cooling in the kitchen, his cousin's toddler was escalating toward a meltdown, and somewhere between the Four Questions and the second cup of wine, Edouard had forgotten something.

He realized it the way you realize a missing stair. The meal had reached its crescendo, the afikoman's turn, and when he reached for the cloth napkin where he thought he'd tucked it, his hand found only a fork. At the start of the Seder he had broken the middle matzah, wrapped the larger piece, and then his uncle had asked him a question about his college deposits, and the piece had simply never left his hand's memory and gone into hiding. A piece of the middle matzah, set aside and hidden for the children to find, and it was the last food eaten at the meal. Nothing could properly conclude without it.

Last spring, before everything, his grandfather had run the Seder from his chair at the head of this same table, and Edouard had watched him hide the afikoman behind the bookshelf with theatrical slowness while the little ones shrieked and pretended not to look. His grandfather's voice had been mild but trenchant that night when Edouard asked why the ritual mattered so much. "You'll see," he had said. "One day the table will be yours and you'll see." Three weeks later the chair at the head of the table was empty, and Edouard's mother had asked him, quietly, in the hallway, whether he would lead this year. He had said yes before he understood what he was agreeing to carry.
