Now Mikaella, his oldest friend, sat across from him watching his face the way she watched proofs on a whiteboard, waiting to see whether he'd catch his own error. He caught it. He stood up, napkin in hand, and did the only thing he could think of.

"I hid it," he announced, "with more skill than usual."

Audrey, his cousin, twelve and merciless, folded her arms. "You didn't hide anything. You've been sitting there the whole time."

"You were watching the Haggadah," Edouard said. "Not me." He walked a slow circuit of the dining room, holding the wrapped piece above his head like a trophy whose location was a state secret, and behind the bookshelf, in the exact gap his grandfather had used, he slid it. His hand trembled slightly and he let it. The children were already out of their chairs.

There was a cost to the improvisation and he knew it. His grandfather's hiding had enfranchised the children, had made them participants in the story rather than an audience for it, and Edouard's version was a forgery of that, an after-the-fact trick. Audrey would find the piece in four minutes, not the usual twenty, because she had watched him place it, and she would know, and he would never know whether she kept the knowledge to herself out of kindness or out of contempt. He handed her the flashlight anyway.

"Remember," he said, "whoever finds it gets to bargain."

"Grandpa always gave five dollars," Audrey said, already moving toward the shelf.

"Grandpa," said Edouard, "is not the one leading this year." It came out sharper than he meant, and the table went quiet around the word, and his grandmother looked at her hands.

Mikaella caught his eye and mouthed, the wine, and he remembered the fourth cup still unpoured, and the schedule his mother had written on the fridge, because the toddler had to be in bed by nine and it was already half past eight. He poured. He blessed. He rushed the part about Elijah's cup, and the door they opened to the night air let in cold that smelled of the neighbor's hyacinths, and for a second he let himself imagine his grandfather walking in, unhurried, taking his seat.

Audrey returned holding the afikoman above her head. "Ten dollars," she said.

"Five," said Edouard, and then, before she could argue, "and you get to hand out the pieces." That was not tradition either. That was his own invention, and he watched her consider it, this redistribution of honor, this small enfranchising of a twelve-year-old who had caught him cheating, and he watched her decide that she liked it.

She broke the matzah and moved around the table, giving each person a fragment, and when she reached their grandmother she bent and put the largest piece in the old woman's palm and closed her fingers over it. It was the last food of the meal; everyone ate their share and no one spoke until the pieces were gone. Edouard looked down at the crumbs on his plate, then up at the head of the table where his grandfather's wine glass still sat, unused, at the empty chair.

"Next year," his grandmother said, "hide it better."

"Next year," Edouard said, "I'll let you hide it."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
story:
The radiator under the window of Room 214 clanked twice before anyone spoke, and Ms. Kerr wrote a single word on the board, then erased it before anyone could copy it down. "You argue like people throwing coats over a puddle," she said. "Each side just wants to get across. Nobody looks at the puddle." She set them in pairs. Marcus got Larry, which was unlucky, because Larry had been furious since the assembly on Friday, when the school announced that senior parking spots would be allocated by lottery instead of grade average.

"It's theft," Larry said. He leaned back until his chair creaked. "I worked four years for my spot. Some kid who failed three classes takes it because he pulled a red ticket."

Marcus had his own position ready, had been holding it all weekend like a stone in his pocket: the lottery is fairer because seniors don't earn public resources, the spots belong to the school, not to the students. He started to say it. Then he stopped, because Ms. Kerr was walking the rows with her arms folded, listening, and something about her silence made him reluctant to be the next person talking past his partner.

"So your claim," Marcus said slowly, "isn't just that you want the spot. It's that effort should determine reward, and if the school breaks that link, then grades stop mattering to anyone. If juniors see seniors rewarded randomly, the whole incentive to work collapses. That's the real stake, right? Not one parking space."

Larry put his chair down on all four legs. "Yeah. That. Why couldn't I say it like that?"

"Because you were busy calling it theft," Marcus said. "That's not an argument, that's a slogan."

From the next row, Kristian turned around. Kristian read philosophy forums the way other people read sports stats, hoarding terms the way Larry hoarded grievances. "You just steelmanned him," Kristian said. "Stating the other side's argument in its strongest form, even stronger than he put it, before you answer it. That's what that's called." Marcus wrote the word in his margin and didn't look at it again for three days.

The trouble was at home, and it arrived on Tuesday night in the form of a curfew. Eleven o'clock on weekends, his father announced, starting immediately, because Marcus had come in at one the previous Saturday without calling. Marcus had prepared his counterattack in the shower: seventeen in September, college in eleven months, adult soon, trust me now or lose me later. Pithy, he'd thought. Devastating, even.

He sat down across the table from his father and, before launching it, heard Kristian's voice in his head like a bad jingle. He set his prepared speech aside, and it cost him something to do it, like uncurling a fist he'd been holding all day.

"Let me see if I've got your side first," Marcus said. "You were awake at one in the morning with no idea where I was. You called twice and I didn't pick up. And your real worry isn't this one night, it's that if you can't reach me now, when I'm under your roof, then what happens when I'm two hours away and something goes wrong and calling me is all you can do. The curfew isn't about controlling me. It's about proving the system still works before you lose the ability to use it."

His father's hand, which had been flat on the table, turned over. He looked at his own palm as though it had said something. "I didn't say it that well," he admitted. "That's better than I put it."

"I know," Marcus said. "That's kind of the point."

There followed a silence that was not hostile, which was itself strange, and in it Marcus noticed that his own argument, the one he'd rehearsed, had quietly fallen apart in his hands. Trust me now or lose me later was a threat wearing the costume of a reason, a circumlocution around the actual fact, which was that he hadn't called and hadn't thought about his father awake at the window until this moment. He could not honestly claim that his freedom to stay out late should not be subjugated to anyone's peace of mind when he had spent the other person's peace of mind without asking.

"So do I still get the curfew?" he asked.

His father poured himself more tea, though the cup was still a third full, which was something he did when buying time. "Eleven on Friday and Saturday," he said. "Midnight if you call by ten and tell me where you are. Not a text. A call."

"And weeknights?"

"We'll see how the weekend goes."

It was not a victory and not a defeat, and Marcus found he could not tell which one he'd even been pursuing anymore. He took his plate to the sink. At the doorway he stopped, one hand on the frame.

"Next time I'll call before you have to."

His father didn't look up from his tea. "Next time," he said, "answer on the second ring."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
story:
Mr. Aquino's classroom smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's scorched dust, and the desks had been pushed into the crooked circle he liked for Friday forums. Laurie sat with her essay folded in thirds under her hand, not reading it, listening. The topic was whether the school should fund a later bus route so students with long commutes could stay for clubs and tutoring. Mira had been talking for two minutes, carefully, about how the current schedule quietly shut out kids from the far side of the county.

"So you're saying we should just spend unlimited money on anyone who wants a ride," Mallory said. She was leaning back, arms crossed, chin lifted toward the window. "That's basically your whole argument. Blank cheque."

"I didn't say unlimited," Mira said. "I said the current route cuts off at five."

"Same thing. You want the school to pay for everything." Mallory turned to the room as if she had already won, and a few people nodded, the easy nod of an audience watching someone get flattened.

Laurie's pen stopped. She looked down at her own notes, where she had been sketching Mira's actual claim, and beside it she wrote: that's not what she said. Her heart did the thing it did before she raised her hand, a small cold plunge, though some part of her found the moment exhilarating too, the way a high dive must feel from the edge. She thought about staying quiet. Mallory was her friend from chemistry lab, the person who saved her a seat at lunch and had once lent her bus fare when her own account ran penurious at the end of the month. That memory made it harder, not easier, to speak.

"That's a straw man," Laurie said, and then, when the room turned, "It's when you attack a weaker, distorted version of what someone said instead of their actual argument, and act like they're the same thing." Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Mira proposed one extra run at five thirty. She didn't propose unlimited anything."

"That's basically the same thing," Mallory said, but quieter.

Laurie turned her notebook around on her knee so only Mallory could see it. On it she had drawn two boxes. In the first: one bus, 5:30, cost. In the second, which she had crossed out hard: money without limit. "If it's the same, this would be in here," she said, tapping the first box, "but it isn't, so we're arguing about a thing nobody said." She could hear how stiff it sounded, and she let it stand, because it was true and because softening it would have made it less true.

Mr. Aquino, who had been leaning against the whiteboard with his arms folded, uncrossed them. "All right," he said. "Then let's argue about the thing somebody said. Mallory, what would you say to the actual proposal?" He didn't praise Laurie, and she was grateful; praise would have made it Mallory's humiliation instead of Mallory's turn.

Mallory was quiet for a second. The radiator ticked. "I'd say we can't afford it," she said finally, sitting up. "The activities budget's already thin, and I actually care about that, because if they take it from activities, they're taking it from the robotics club, which is mine." There it was, Laurie thought: the want underneath the bluster. Mallory wasn't against buses. She was afraid of losing her club, and she had dressed that fear up as a principle and hurled it at the nearest target.

"Then say that," Laurie said. "Say, if the money comes from activities, I'm against it, and if it comes from somewhere else, maybe I'm not. That's an actual position. I can argue with that." She heard herself building the conditional as she spoke, the if shaping itself in her mouth, and it felt like handing Mallory a plank across the gap between them rather than a shove.

Mallory studied her for a moment. "If it comes from the surplus in the facilities line," she said slowly, "then fine, I'd vote for it. But only that."

"Only that," Mira agreed, and something in the room loosened, the way air does after a storm cell passes. Mr. Aquino wrote "facilities surplus?" on the board and underlined it twice.

Laurie didn't feel entirely clean about it. She had corrected her friend in front of thirty people, and she knew Mallory would remember that on Monday, at the lunch table, in the small currency of saved seats and borrowed fare. There was also a question she couldn't answer: whether she had been fair or merely quick, whether the line between a distorted argument and an honest simplification was as bright as she had claimed. She turned back to her notes and wrote, at the bottom, in smaller letters: check with M. later. When the bell rang, Mallory gathered her bag slowly, and Laurie waited by the door, holding it open, notebook under her arm.

"Robotics meets Tuesday," Mallory said, not quite looking at her. "We need someone who can actually write the grant summary. You want it or not?"

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month.
story:
Makayla taped the tenth sheet to the cabin wall and stepped back until her heels hit Anne's bunk. Nine of the pieces were the lake at dusk, done in oil pastel, each one from the same flat rock by the dock. The tenth was a page of notes, half erased, and she was starting to think it didn't count.

"That's not a lake," Blaine said from the doorway, holding two popsicles he'd clearly traded for. "That's a lake nine times."

"That's the assignment." Makayla peeled the tape from the tenth sheet before it could tear. "Ten artworks, one theme, artist's statement. Ms. Joseph wants a body of work, not a scrapbook." She heard herself sounding more certain than she was. The truth was she'd chosen the lake because it was the only thing she could see from the rock, and because after her grandfather died in March, the months at home had felt like an interregnum, a stretch with no proper government, and the lake at dusk was the only thing that had looked the same two evenings in a row.

Blaine handed her a popsicle and sat on the floor. "So what's your statement say?"

"It says I'm interested in repetition." She said it flatly, the way you repeat a word until it stops meaning anything.

At critique that afternoon, Ms. Joseph walked the row of easels without touching anything. When she reached Makayla's she stopped for a long time, arms crossed, and then said only, "Who is this for?" and moved on. The question sat in Makayla's chest like a swallowed stone. She knew what Ms. Joseph meant. The camp show was in three weeks, and families and local artists came, and some pieces sold. Blaine had sold a watercolor last summer, a diaphanous thing of birches that a woman from town bought for forty dollars. Blaine hadn't stopped mentioning it.

That night, while the cabin slept, Makayla went to the camp's small library, really a shelf in the mess hall, and pulled down the fattest book on Monet because her mother had once said the word "series" about him and she'd pretended to know what it meant. She read by the light of the drink machine. Monet had shown fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month. Fifteen pictures of the same stacks of grain. She turned back a page and read it again, then copied it onto her hand because she'd left her sketchbook in the cabin.

She found Blaine at breakfast and put her hand, notes side up, on his tray. "Fifteen," she said. "Same haystacks. Most of them sold within a month."

Blaine studied her palm while eating his eggs. "So people will buy nine lakes?"

"That's not the point. The point is a gallery hung fifteen of the same subject and people wanted them." She hadn't decided yet whether it was the point or not. She kept recalibrating as she said it, moving between the version where the fact proved her idea and the version where it proved nothing, where 1891 buyers were not camp families, where fifteen haystacks in a Paris gallery were not nine pastels on a plywood table by a canoe rack.

She spent the afternoon on the flat rock instead of in the studio. The lake did what it did, which was nothing and everything, the light going from pewter to copper to a color she didn't have a name for. She thought about her grandfather's apartment, how after the funeral her mother had wanted to sort it in a weekend and her aunt had wanted to leave it untouched for a year, and how Makayla, seventeen then, had said nothing. She could draw the lake a hundred times and it would never say what she'd failed to say in that apartment. But it could hold the place where the saying should have been. That was different. That might even be a statement.

On the last critique day, Ms. Joseph stopped at Makayla's row again. Nine lakes, then, in the end, because Makayla had spent two studio periods reworking the fifth piece instead of replacing the notes page, and a tenth blank sheet taped up at the end with a penciled title: To Be Continued.

"Ten?" Ms. Joseph asked.

"Ten," Makayla said. "The tenth one's just quiet."

Ms. Joseph looked at the blank sheet, then at the lake, then back. Anne, sitting cross-legged on the floor with her portfolio in her lap, whispered, "I'd buy the copper one," and Blaine said, "Forty dollars," and Makayla laughed, and Ms. Joseph wrote something in her notebook and moved on.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
story:
Maelle had spread the whole kitchen table with her campaign: the print of The Two Fridas propped against the sugar bowl, her sketchbook open beside it, three pens, a pot of tea going cold, and a page of notes so prolix that Evan, arriving on time for once, read the first line and sat down slowly, as if bracing.

"You wrote a paragraph on the clouds," he said.

"The clouds matter. They're part of the composition. Everything in the frame is doing work, that's the whole point of formal analysis. You look at colour, composition, symbolism, and you build the critique from what's actually there instead of just saying it made you feel sad."

"Where would anyone get the idea it made you feel sad," Evan said, and stole a biscuit.

The assignment from Ms. MacLeod was due Monday, and Maelle had been circling it for two days. Eve-Marie, over text, had called the method a technocracy of looking, some algorithm you fed a painting into so it could spit out a tidy verdict, and Maelle had typed and deleted three replies before giving up and trying to just do the work. Formal analysis, she kept reminding herself, was not a machine for killing feeling. It was a way of being accountable to the object. If she said the painting was about loneliness, she had to be able to point at where loneliness lived in it.

She pulled the sketchbook toward her and began transcribing the composition into simple shapes, because that was a trick she'd read about: reduce the figures to geometry and see what the painting was actually built on. Two women, seated, holding hands on the right side. One in white, one in blue. She drew the white dress large and airy, the blue dress smaller and contained, and then she paused, squinting at the print, and leaned in so close her nose nearly touched Frida's unibrow.

"Evan. Evan, look at this."

"What am I looking at."

"Both of them. Their hearts." She tapped the print. Both women's chests were open, and the hearts were visible, exposed, one to each Frida. She took the red pen and, on her sketch, traced a single blood vessel running out of the heart of the Frida in blue, winding down through their joined hands and up into the heart of the Frida in white. "It's one line. The whole connection, it's one vessel. It goes through their hands and their hearts, that's the only thing holding them together."

Evan put his head briefly on the table. "You found that with a red pen and a postcard."

"I found that with rigorous formal analysis," Maelle said, but her voice had gone quiet. She sat back and looked at her own sketch, at the red thread she had drawn, and something rearranged itself in her head with an almost audible click. Because here was the thing: she could describe the line as composition, a diagonal connecting the two figures, unifying the halves of the canvas. She could describe it as symbolism, the shared life, the selves that could not be severed. And the line did not care which vocabulary she used. It was both, at once, and neither description was wrong, and neither was enough.

"That's the essay," she said.

"Which one, the sad one or the algorithm one?"

"It's the one where the analysis can't finish. I say what the line does formally, I say what it means, and then I say the line outruns both of them." She was already writing, fast, the pen skating. She felt honest about it, which was the strange part. She was not resolving anything. She was keeping the uncertainty on the page, in ink, where Ms. MacLeod would have to look at it.

On Monday the essay came back with a single comment in the margin, in Ms. MacLeod's narrow green handwriting, and Maelle read it at the kitchen table with Evan reading over her shoulder, which she permitted only because the tea was good. The comment said: rigorous, argued, and brave enough not to close. Then, at the bottom, the mark. Maelle stared at it.

"It's the same grade Eve-Marie got," she said.

"So?"

"Eve-Marie wrote hers on why formal analysis fails. Two hundred words. She called it a technocracy and turned it in." Maelle put the page down and laughed, once, a short shocked sound. "We argued from opposite ends and landed in the same place."

Evan picked up the postcard, held it at arm's length, and traced the little red thread through the joined hands with one fingertip, very carefully, like a man defusing something. "So the vessel connects them," he said, "and the grade connects you two."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Brody counted the turnovers out loud, the way Ms. Kaminski had told him to, one hand curled around a clipboard he felt ridiculous holding. Eleven. In forty minutes, the under-twelve team had lost the ball eleven times on passes that never arrived, each one cut out by a defender's foot sliding across the grass. The kids looked at him afterward with the flat patience of people who already believed the practice would be pointless, and one boy named nothing at all kicked a cone into the hedge and walked to the far goal to sit alone, disaffected, arms around his knees.

He wanted to fix it. That was the whole assignment, the reason Ms. Kaminski had signed him up for the coaching practicum instead of the recycling committee: plan drills that address a specific weakness, not just run them until dark. But the weakness had a shape he couldn't name yet, something about low, lazy balls rolling straight through the legs of the other team, and every drill he'd invented so far had only repeated the problem at slower speed.

That night his dad had the hockey game on, volume low, and Brody sat down with his notebook mostly to avoid his homework. A winger carried the puck along the boards, drew two defenders, and then flicked it so that it rose just off the ice, sailed flat over the outstretched stick of the man sprawled in its path, and settled down onto a teammate's blade without so much as a bounce. The announcer called it a saucer pass, and Brody wrote the words down before he thought about why.

At lunch the next day he was still writing, and Faith leaned across the table to read upside down, which she did without asking. "That's hockey," she said. "You're coaching soccer."

"I know what I'm coaching."

"Do you," said Amalia, who had played striker since she was eight and regarded most of Brody's ideas with a scholar's skepticism. "In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands right on the receiver's blade. That's the whole point, it goes over the stick. There's no sticks in soccer."

"There's feet," Brody said. "Feet get in the way exactly like sticks do." Amalia tilted her head, considering, which from her was nearly applause, and Faith stole a fry.

Saturday he brought a bag of tennis balls, lighter than soccer balls, easier to chip. He set cones as defenders' legs across the middle third and told the kids the ball had to go over the cones and come down inside a chalked square, that it should land, not bounce away. The boy from the hedge came back without being asked, which Brody pretended not to notice. The first attempts were disasters, one sailing over the fence and costing Brody two minutes and a favor from the groundskeeper, but by the third rotation a small kid named after nobody in particular lofted a ball that cleared three cones, dropped dead in the square, and rolled gently into her teammate's stride.

The problem, Brody discovered, was that he now had two truths and they didn't fit together. Elevation beat the defenders' feet, sure, but a chipped ball in the air is slow and readable, and Amalia had stood at the fence watching the last ten minutes, and when she came over she said, "You've fixed the blocked passes and eviscerated your own tempo. They'll get intercepted in the air now." He hated that she was right and said so, which made her laugh.

He put it to the kids as a vote, a small plebiscite conducted with raised hands and one raised water bottle: chip only when a defender's leg is directly in the passing lane, keep everything else on the ground and quick. The kid from the hedge voted yes twice, one hand and then the bottle, and Brody let it stand. Ms. Kaminski watched the last scrimmage from the touchline, saying nothing, and twice the small girl clipped a ball over a sliding challenge that landed rolling at someone's feet, and twice the whole team made a sound like something had been settled.

Not everything was settled. In the final minute a chipped pass hung too long, and a defender headed it away easily, and the boy from the hedge turned to Brody with his palms up, waiting for the answer. Brody raised one hand: hold, meaning he didn't know yet, meaning next week, meaning maybe never entirely. The boy lowered his palms, jogged back to the center circle, and tapped the ball into play.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
The pharmacy smelled of floor cleaner and cough drops, and the blood pressure machine stood between the film counter and the batteries like something between a joke and a dare. Anthony's mother sat down on the little stool anyway, because she had a headache and because the machine was free and because, as she said, it beat standing in the prescription line doing nothing. She pushed up her sleeve, slid her arm into the cuff, and sat very still while the machine hummed and tightened and slowly let go. The numbers came up on the screen: 125 over 78.

"That's fine, right?" she said, already reaching for her purse.

Anthony copied the numbers into his phone before the screen cleared. "I don't know. We just did this in Mr. Desir's class. I mostly remember the pictures of arteries."

"Then you remember more than I do. Come on, they called my name."

But he hung back a step. Mr. Desir had assigned them each a real reading from a real person, with a paragraph explaining what category it fell into and how diet and exercise changed it, due Friday. Anthony had been planning to use his own reading from the gym, taken casually, half a joke. Now he had his mother's numbers, and a small cold feeling that he couldn't apportion between schoolwork and worry. He texted Sydnee from the deodorant aisle while his mother waited at the counter.

"my mom got 125/78 at the walgreens machine. is that normal or what"

The reply came fast, as Sydnee's replies always did, as if she'd been holding the answer in her mouth. It came in pieces, which was how Sydnee thought, out loud and sideways.

"ok so we have the 2017 american guideline sheet. there's a category called elevated. it's systolic 120 to 129 AND diastolic below 80."

then: "your mom is 125 systolic. 78 diastolic."

then: "both fit."

then: "so that's elevated, not normal. it's below the numbers for actual hypertension but it's not nothing either."

"you sure"

"i'm reading it off the sheet right now. avery's here, she's nodding. also avery says stop texting during pharmacy hours."

Anthony stood there with the message open, thumb hovering. Below the conversation was the paragraph Mr. Desir wanted: explain how diet and exercise change it. He knew the shape of that answer, the reduced salt, the walks, the vegetables that neither he nor his mother especially wanted. It had seemed abstract in class, a thing that happened to hypothetical people in worksheets. Now it had his mother's arm in it.

In the car he showed her the texts. "It's called elevated," he said. "It's a real category. You should probably make an appointment."

She looked at the screen at a red light longer than he liked. "The machine at the pharmacy," she said. "Those things sit there all day. Some man coughed on that cuff last week, I watched him." But when they got home she took the frozen lasagna out of the oven plans anyway and put it back in the freezer, and made rice and the sad-looking broccoli, and afterward they walked around the block twice because Anthony asked, and once more because she said the air felt good. He noticed, walking, that he had never once walked with just her, without an errand attached, and that the errand-less walking was better, and that this observation felt almost indecorous, like eavesdropping on her.

That night he wrote the paragraph for Mr. Desir. He wrote that his subject's reading of 125 over 78 fell into the category called elevated, that the guideline defined it as a systolic of 120 to 129 with a diastolic below 80, and that sodium reduction, aerobic activity and dietary change were the standard first responses. Then he stopped, because the next sentence he'd drafted began "therefore, my mother," and he didn't know whether that was germane or just dramatic, whether a number on a pharmacy machine could carry that much weight. He remembered being eight and her carrying him half a mile to the clinic when he sprained his ankle, certain that the pain would incapacitate him forever, and how she hadn't even changed her breathing. He remembered smaller things too, worse ones, times he hadn't helped when helping would have been easy. He left the last part blank and went to sleep.

On Friday Mr. Desir collected the paragraphs and read Anthony's, and said only, "You'll have your mother sign the permission slip for the unit on family health history," and moved on, which was either a judgment or the absence of one. Sydnee caught him in the hall. "So did she make the appointment?" she asked.

"Tuesday," Anthony said. "I'm driving her. She says I need the hours anyway."

Saturday morning his mother waved the folded newspaper at him from the kitchen table. "Avery's mother is a nurse, you know. I called her Thursday. She says those machines read high if the cuff's over a sleeve, and I had my sweater pushed up but not off." She set the paper down and turned back to the stove, where something with garlic was happening. "I took it again yesterday at the fire station. One eighteen over seventy-four."

Anthony looked at his paragraph, still in his bag, already handed in, already graded, the category called elevated, and then at the broccoli she was chopping for tonight, because she had decided she liked it now.

"So do we still go for the walk?" he asked.

"Two blocks," she said, "and you're pushing the pace."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
The mayonnaise broke on the third Saturday of Natalie's self-imposed summer of competence, which was how she had privately begun to think of the months before college applications consumed everything. She had come to her grandmother's house with a plan: she would cook dinner, all of it, without help, because her grandmother had been forgetting things lately and someone needed to start carrying more of the weight. That was the version Natalie told herself. The truer version was that she wanted proof, some concrete evidence she could do hard things, and a dinner seemed like a manageable seismic event compared with everything else looming.

She stood at the counter with the mixer running, pouring oil in a thin stream the way the video had shown, and for a while it worked, the yellow mixture thickening into something that looked almost right. Then, between one breath and the next, it turned. The whole bowl went glossy and loose, oil pooling at the edges, a curdled slick that no amount of whipping would pull back together. Jase, who had come along partly for the ride and partly because his own house was empty, leaned over her shoulder and pronounced it ruined. "It's soup," he said. "Mayonnaise soup."

Natalie's first instinct was to throw it out and start over, which was her instinct about most failures, and she was reaching for the sink when her grandmother came in from the garden with dirt still under her nails. Her grandmother looked into the bowl for a long moment, the way she looked at crossword clues she used to solve instantly, and Natalie felt the familiar tightness in her chest, the fear that this, too, would be one of the things that had gone missing.

"You pushed it too fast," her grandmother said finally. "It happens. Get me another egg."

Kasey arrived halfway through the rescue, sent by her mother with a bag of tomatoes nobody wanted, and she stood in the doorway taking in the scene: Natalie's grandmother cracking a single yolk into a clean bowl, Natalie beating it, then spooning the broken mixture in slowly, spoonful by spoonful, while the older woman rested a hand on the counter to steady herself. Nobody spoke during the critical minutes. Then, impossibly, the sauce came back, creamy and pale, holding together in a way Natalie could not immediately account for.

Her grandmother explained only in fragments, the way she explained things now, offering pieces and letting Natalie assemble them. She said the word "emulsifiers" once, tapping the bowl. She said the lecithin and the proteins in the yolk were what held the tiny oil droplets suspended in the water so the sauce did not separate, and then she went to sit down, the effort of even that much speech visible in her shoulders. Natalie stood there with the mixer and thought about it. Oil and water refusing each other, and then something small and yellow stepping between them, holding everything in suspension. She did not say any of this out loud.

Later, while the chicken roasted, Natalie sat on the back steps with Jase and Kasey, who had divided the tomatoes between them and were arguing about whether their classmates' habit of sorting people into types was a form of science or a form of laziness. Kasey, who wanted to study psychology, defended taxonomy, the usefulness of categories; Jase said categories were just excuses people made for not looking closely. Natalie found herself on both sides at once. She thought about how she had wanted tonight to prove something clean about herself, and how instead the evening had broken and been brought back with help, with her grandmother's memory arriving in pieces, with the whole dinner depending on things she could not have done alone.

She went back inside to check the oven and found her grandmother at the table with two glasses of water, one placed at Natalie's seat. They sat together without talking much. Natalie asked whether the mayonnaise trick was something her grandmother's mother had taught her, and her grandmother said it was, then added, after a pause, that she might not remember it next time. Natalie said that was fine, because now one of them did.

Dinner was late and slightly overbrown on one edge of the pan, and the mayonnaise, spooned over the tomatoes Kasey had sliced, held. Jase took a second helping without commenting, which was his highest available compliment. Afterward Natalie washed the dishes alone by choice, her grandmother drying beside her, their hands passing plates back and forth in a rhythm that needed no arranging. When the last bowl was done, her grandmother squeezed the towel dry, hung it on the oven door, and said, "Same time next Saturday, then."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
story:
I have never in my life made an arithmetic error, which is a thing I told Alexie twice on the bus and would tell anyone who asked, and my chemistry worksheet was going to prove it. That was the plan for Saturday afternoon anyway: sit at Grandpa's kitchen table, where nobody bothers you, and finish the mole problems before dinner. Grandpa's house smelled like coffee and the lemon polish he put on everything twice a week, and Grandpa himself sat in the armchair by the window being taciturn, which in his case meant answering questions with his eyebrows.

The worksheet was the latest skirmish in a long war. Ms. Vu had assigned it Friday with the announcement that stoichiometry was where chemistry stopped being vocabulary and started being arithmetic, and half the class had groaned, and I had not, because arithmetic was not my nemesis. My nemesis, if I had one, was Ms. Vu's habit of writing "see me" in red pen on problems I knew were right. Anyway. I spread out my paper, sharpened two pencils to avoid starting, and started.

The problem was straightforward. Given so many grams of a reactant, calculate the moles of carbon dioxide formed. You needed the molar mass of carbon dioxide first, and I remembered the rule the way I remembered most things, confidently and possibly incorrectly: the molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula. Carbon was 12.01. Oxygen was 16.00. I wrote 28.01 at the side of the page, underlined it, and proceeded to the rest of the problem with the composure of a person who has never once been wrong about a number.

My phone buzzed. Alexie, from across town, having apparently finished her worksheet already: "how many moles did u get for #4." I sent my answer. Three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared. "that's not what I got." I typed back that she should check her work, then deleted it, because Alexie had checked her work, was famous for checking her work, had once found an error in the seating chart. I sat with my pencil in my teeth.

The kitchen clock ticked the way clocks do in houses where nobody talks much. Grandma was upstairs, and Grandpa turned a page of his newspaper, and I re-read my own line, 28.01, and found nothing wrong with it, because you never do. Then Franco texted the class group chat a photograph of his paper with "IS THIS RIGHT" and no other words, and there it was, his setup, exactly like mine except for one thing: where I had written 28.01 he had written 44.01, and under it, in his terrible handwriting, "12.01 plus two times 16.00."

I looked at the formula. CO2. One carbon, and then the little two that I had read a hundred times this year and apparently skipped every single time, the way you skip a step that isn't there. Two oxygens. Two times 16.00. I did it again, slowly, as though the numbers might have moved: 12.01 plus 32.00, which is 44.01 grams per mole. I checked it against Franco's number. Then, because I trust Franco exactly as far as I can add, I checked it against the periodic table printed inside my notebook cover, 16.00, oxygen, and then the paper in front of me, and the two agreed for once.

This would have been the moment to tell Alexie she was right, and I did consider it. Instead I recalculated the whole problem, got a mole answer that matched hers exactly, and sat back with the sour satisfaction of someone whose error has been committed by the universe on his behalf. There was no denying the arithmetic, obviously. The little two had simply failed to make itself known, a printing problem, possibly a conspiracy.

Grandpa lowered the newspaper one inch. He had been watching, I realized, the way he watched everything, without comment, and now he looked at my paper, at the crossed-out 28.01, at the 44.01 beside it, and raised both eyebrows, which in his language was a full paragraph.

"It was the oxygen," I said. "There's two of them."

He set the newspaper down, came over, and tapped the little subscript two twice with one finger, then went back to his chair. On the way he picked up my eraser, which had rolled to the edge of the table, and set it beside my hand, and that was all, and somehow it was more annoying than anything Ms. Vu had ever written in red.

I redid the remaining four problems with the doubled oxygen, and my answers kept agreeing with Alexie's, which was either corroboration or a sign that she was copying my error rate in advance. I photographed the page and sent it to her without a message, and she sent back a single thumbs up, and I decided that counted as an apology on both sides, or would, eventually, if she brought it up, which she would, at school, in front of Franco.

At dinner Grandma asked how the homework had gone, and I said it had gone fine, which was true by then, more or less, except for the part where I had spent twenty minutes being certain about the one thing in the world I was wrong about. Grandpa salted his potatoes. The clock went on ticking in the other room, twice as fast as it should have, now that I thought about it, and I got up to go look at it.
